---
title: "abstract"
---

INTRODUCTION: Dementia develops over decades, yet most epigenome-wide studies contrast prevalent cases with controls and cannot establish whether blood methylation alterations precede clinical progression or follow it.

METHODS: We profiled baseline blood DNA methylation in 2,491 participants of the Age, Gene/Environment Susceptibility-Reykjavik Study (mean age 76 years), followed up to 13.4 years and adjudicated into six clinical stages: stable normal cognition, two mild cognitive impairment (MCI) trajectories, two prospective transitions to dementia, and prevalent dementia. Differentially methylated positions were summarized as latent dimensions with a variational autoencoder (VAE) and UMAP.

RESULTS: Among participants who were cognitively normal at baseline, methylation had already diverged in opposite directions: profiles were concordant with prevalent dementia in those who later developed dementia (*r* = 0.87) but inverted in those who progressed only to MCI (no further deterioration throughout the follow-up, *r* = [−0.48]{.rev}). 403 CpG sites reached genome-wide significance in at least one stage. Both VAE and UMAP recovered a continuous latent trajectory tracking clinical [progression]{.rev}, and ordered *APOE* genotypes by risk role without genotype data. Effect sizes were concordant with independent Alzheimer's disease cohorts. Enrichment was stage-specific: synaptic, extracellular matrix and immune processes at the earliest transition, hypoxia response in stable MCI, and cell-cycle regulation in prevalent dementia.

DISCUSSION: Blood methylation [differed among the groups]{.rev} years before diagnosis. Rather than a single intermediate state between normal cognition and dementia, MCI comprised courses running in opposite directions, and early and late stages [were enriched for different biological processes]{.rev}.
